title: Adult female pythons cause the most trouble in Florida
summary:
The Burmese python is such a problem for Florida that it is legal to hunt the massive invasive species throughout the year. The state even hosts an annual 10-day competition that challenges participants to catch as many snakes as possible. But a free-for-all approach may not be the best way to cull Florida's estimated 100,000-300,000 of these predators. In a study published in the journal Ecological Applications, conservationists argue that to make a real dent, people need to be more selective about their targets.

"Our previous work treated all Burmese pythons as contributing equally to the population," University of Florida ecologist Alex Romer said. "But removing the biggest female we've ever caught is very different from removing a tiny snake that might not survive next year."

Romer and his colleagues analyzed data from the South Florida Water Management District's Python Elimination Program to develop a new system called the Weighted Removal Index (WRI). Points are awarded to a snake depending on factors including its age, sex and what time of year it was removed. Younger snakes do not get a higher ranking because many do not survive long enough to breed, so hunters' efforts are better directed elsewhere. For the largest impact, the researchers suggest pursuing mature female pythons.

"Every Burmese python removed is a win for the Everglades, but targeting large reproductive females is likely to reduce the population most effectively," explained University of Florida invasive ecologist Melissa Miller. "The idea is that a big female might be worth 100 arbitrary ecological points, while a little snake might be worth five," added Romer.

The team believes the strategy could be especially successful along regional borders of the python invasion. An adult female regularly lays around 70 eggs at a time, so removing them from these sites will slow their offspring's expansion into new areas.

The findings also pointed to an unexpected conclusion. Florida runs its annual python hunting challenge in the summer, but organizers may want to consider rescheduling it for winter. Data indicates that although fewer pythons are removed in months like January or February, their WRI ratings are much higher because they are mostly adults.

"Combining and plugging this knowledge into models...can be a game changer that can really make a difference in the battle to combat these invaders," added biologist and study co-author Sergio Balaguera-Reina.
why_it_matters: The study suggests that the same amount of effort may help the environment more if hunters focus on the snakes that will have the biggest effect on the python population.

questions.question: What did Romer say earlier work had assumed?
options: That hunters should only catch young snakes
That all Burmese pythons contributed equally to the population
That only the biggest females mattered at all
That the time of year changed nothing
questions.correct_answer: That all Burmese pythons contributed equally to the population

questions.question: Which factors affect a snake's points in the WRI?
options: Its weight, its speed and how it hunts
Its habitat, its diet and its home range
Its age, its sex and the time of year it was removed
Its color, its length and where it was found
questions.correct_answer: Its age, its sex and the time of year it was removed

questions.question: Why might winter removals score higher?
options: The pythons removed then are mostly adults
The snakes grow larger in cold months
More pythons are removed in the winter
The hunters are paid extra for each snake
questions.correct_answer: The pythons removed then are mostly adults
